To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the phosphoproteomics of human CD34+ progenitor cells is significantly different from that of T cells, pointing toward the importance of specific kinase‐mediated pathways in the regulation of hematopoietic fate.

we have used an empirically optimized phosphoproteome enrichment strategy with 2D liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry to identify 3574 putatively phosphorylated proteins, including 15 533 phosphopeptides, in human CD34(+) hematopoietic cells.

we have developed and validated a novel phosphoproteomics approach to study the human CD34+ cell population, which is the main target for stem cell therapies in the treatment of hematological malignancies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a large‐scale phosphoproteomics workflow to investigate the signaling network underlying hematopoietic fate decisions.
the development of an integrated network‐based analysis strategy to study signaling in human CD 34+ hematopoetic progenitor cells by phosphoproteome analysis.
the identification and quantitation of phosphorylation events in a human CD34+ progenitor cell population.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data presented here provide a comprehensive, large‐scale phosphoproteome analysis of human CD34+ cells and a valuable resource for future investigations.

the phosphoproteomic approach described herein provides a robust and reproducible method for large‐scale identification and quantitation of phosphorylation sites in CD34+ hematologic stem cells, with the capacity to identify novel phosphorylation sites and pathways in these cells.
the phosphoproteomics approach described in this study has the potential to be a powerful and versatile tool in the study of human HSPC biology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the application of this phosphoproteomics strategy has provided the first global phosphoproteome map of a human hematopoietically enriched cell population and revealed a number of novel candidate substrates of key signaling cascades that are important in the regulation of human HSPCs. © 2011 The Authors.
we have developed a robust, large‐scale phosphoproteomics platform that can be applied to the analysis of human HSPC.

we have established a robust, high‐throughput, and high‐coverage phosphopeptide enrichment strategy that has enabled the identification of thousands of unique phosphopeptides and phosphoproteins in human HSPC, and that we have applied this strategy to identify a set of phosphopeptide motifs and signaling pathways that may have important roles in the regulation of HSPC fate.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the phosphopeptide‐enriched fraction of CD34+ HPCs can be used to identify novel signaling pathway substrates and to map out the phosphoproteomes of human HSPCs, which may be of use in the study of human hematopoietics.
the application of large‐scale phosphoproteomics in combination with pathway analysis can be used to gain insights into signaling pathways and kinase‐substrate interactions that regulate human HSPCs.

the combination of a robust, large‐scale enrichment strategy with high throughput, sensitive MS/MS screening can be applied to characterize signaling networks in primary human cells and that this approach can be extended to study signaling in other primary cells and tissues, including those that are difficult to culture.
